title: Ask the Graph, Not the Document: Clinical Trial Protocols as a Knowledge Graph
description:
Ask the Graph, Not the Document: Clinical Trial Protocols as a Knowledge Graph

An LLM will answer a question about a clinical study protocol with a plausible passage from a document. In a regulated domain, a reviewer needs more: which standard the answer came from, which version, and whose definition was applied.

A protocol defines who is eligible, which activities and assessments are performed, when they occur, and how all of it evolves across versions and amendments. CDISC USDM, CDISC Biomedical Concepts and Digital Data Flow (DDF) keep that information structured and traceable. Yet each standard tends to enter at a different stage, each producing its own representation of the study, while the connecting work is reconstructed by hand, again and again.

Fan Ji and Michael Shulze of Capgemini present an ontology-backed knowledge graph, deployed in an enterprise pharmaceutical environment, that makes those connections explicit.

The architecture:

Ontology structures are derived from clinical data standards rather than hand-crafted
Cross-standard alignment becomes a versioned bridge that can be reviewed and governed, instead of a mapping buried in transformation code
LLM-assisted extraction proposes candidate content; deterministic validation, terminology reconciliation, provenance capture and expert review decide what enters the graph
Gaps and conflicts are surfaced, never silently absorbed
The discipline that kept it from becoming a multi-year modelling exercise: competency questions first. Stakeholders defined them up front, for example "How did protocol amendments affect the Schedule of Activities?" The session follows that one question from extraction and terminology resolution through alignment, ingestion, traversal, provenance inspection and expert review.

The graph serves two readers. People receive answers traceable to source definitions. Agents receive structured, version-aware knowledge to traverse rather than infer from document fragments.

Evaluated with real protocol content and real users, the work also reports where standards disagree, where terminology resists automatic resolution, and where LLM extraction is confidently wrong.
